At LM sites, environmental clean-up has been completed, or treatment systems for groundwater are in place. At more than half of the sites, LM performs long-term surveillance and monitoring to make certain that remedies continue to protect public health and the environment. Considered Sites Overview The Considered Sites Database provides information about sites that were formerly used in the nation’s nuclear weapons and early atomic energy programs and had the potential for residual radioactive contamination. Historic Sites Some LM sites have associated listings on the National Register of Historic Places in recognition of their significance in American history. Get our Newsletter! Dusky shark, Carcharhinus obscurus ( CC-BY-NC-ND-2.0 ) Richard Ling An app tells beachgoers in Massachusetts and Maine if a shark has entered the area. Fishermen in Delaware check their phones to avoid accidentally catching endangered Atlantic sturgeon. Dwindling American shad, once cut off from their spawning grounds by dams, are returning in droves. Each of these stories became possible in part because of tiny “acoustic telemetry” tags and a vast network of researchers deploying them along the East Coast of the U.S. With acoustic telemetry technology, each tag emits a unique, ultrasonic “ping.” Along the Eastern seaboard, thousands of electronic receivers are listening for those pings, ready to detect any tagged animal that swims within about half a kilometer. Researchers in the Atlantic Cooperative Telemetry Network , or “ACT” for short, have been tagging animals for over two decades. Now managed by the Smithsonian Environmental Research Center , the network unites scientists from over 120 organizations from Maine to North Carolina. pages.title: Ski the Italian Dolomites on a hut-to-hut mountain safari | National Geographic
pages.description: The Dolomites are famed for their elegant ski resorts. But there’s another way to see these uniquely craggy peaks, by spending a week skiing between rifugi, spending silent, snowy nights in these remote mountain huts.
pages.text: Ski the Italian Dolomites on a hut-to-hut mountain safari | National Geographic TRAVEL Ski the Italian Dolomites on a hut-to-hut mountain safari The Dolomites are famed for their elegant ski resorts. But there’s another way to see these uniquely craggy peaks, by spending a week skiing between rifugi , spending silent, snowy nights in these remote mountain huts. Rifugio Lagazuoi offers refuge to skiers descending the namesake peak in the Dolomites. Manaz Productions By Katilena Dartford Published April 29, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Rifugio Lagazuoi crowns the mountain. The hut’s dark timber frame stands out against the pale rock and white snow that had drifted down overnight. This isn’t just any mountain. Here in the Dolomites are echoes of endurance; of the men who fought here in 1915, during the ‘White War’ between Italy and Austria-Hungary, when up to 12 metres of snow fell, and far harsher conditions prevailed. Throughout that winter, soldiers traversed breakneck ridges, tunnelling into them to detonate explosives, reshaping the mountain — a high-altitude frontline. It’s early January and exceptionally cold, intensified by the bone-chilling history. I double up my thermals before skiing into the Hidden Valley which descends from the hut, down the northwest side of 2,835m Lagazuoi peak. “You’re standing where people lived, fought and died,” says Tim Hudson, a silver-haired Yorkshireman who co-founded specialist ski company Inspired Italy. We’ve paused on the side of the slope, not in remembrance or ritual, but simply to listen.

pages.text: Skipper Bryce sets new Scotland run record in win over UAE - BBC Sport Image source, ICC/Getty Image caption, Kathyrn Bryce is now Scotland's leading female run-scorer Published 15 November 2026 ICC Women's Emerging Nations Trophy United Arab Emirates 138-4 (20 overs): Oza 64, Hotchandani 43; Gordon 2-24 Scotland 142-3 (18.1 overs): K Bryce 51, S Bryce 43; Dharnidharka 2-22 Scotland win by seven wickets Captain Kathyrn Bryce became Scotland Women's all-time leading run scorer as she hit an unbeaten half century in a seven-wicket win over host nation United Arab Emirates at the ICC Women's Emerging Nations Trophy. The skipper hit seven fours on her way to 51 not out as Scotland reached 142-3 with 11 balls to spare. It takes her international run total to 3562, one more than Kari Carswell. Her sister, Sarah Bryce, made 43, batting at number three after Darcey Carter's departure in the first over. Katherine Fraser added 15, with Pippa Sproul on 16 not out. Batting first, captain Esha Oza led the way with 64 not out as UAE reached 138-4 in their 20 overs. Heena Hotchandani added 43 before she was one of two batters to be stumped by wicketkeeper Sarah Bryce from the bowling of Kirstie Gordon. Having previously beaten Papua New Guinea and lost to Sri Lanka, Scotland sit second in Group A and are assured of a place in the Super Six stage. Scotland conclude their group games against Ireland on Wednesday. pages.text: Skylar Wallace hits three home runs for AUSL Bandits Skip to Content View this post on Instagram Skylar Wallace has been crushing pitches all season long in the Athletes Unlimited Softball League. On Thursday, her power at the plate put her in the AUSL history books. The Chicago Bandits infielder became the first player in league history to homer three times in a game. She achieved the feat during the Bandits’ 15-7 victory over the Carolina Blaze. Wallace lined a two-run dinger just beyond the right-field wall in the second inning, hit a three-run homer to left-center field in the third and added a no-doubt solo shot to right in the sixth. Even when she wasn’t hitting balls out of the yard, Wallace was still doing damage at the dish. She also had a single and an RBI double during her five-hit, seven-RBI performance. Over the past two days against the Blaze, Wallace has gone 9-for-10 with four home runs, nine RBIs and nine runs scored in a pair of Bandits victories. Chicago’s win on Wednesday clinched its spot in the AUSL postseason for the second straight year.

Photograph: Anton Melik Geographical Institute Glaciers Slovenia mourns loss of glacier on its highest peak after scorching summer Extreme heat accelerated disappearance of Triglav glacier from mountain revered as a symbol of Slovenian identity Ajit Niranjan Europe environment correspondent Tue 27 Oct 2026 13.08 EDT Last modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 09.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The final ice patch has vanished from Slovenia’s Triglav glacier, the latest Alpine casualty of Europe’s scorching summer. The once mighty ice mass lost 93% of its surface area between 1983 and 2003, shrinking to cover less than a hectare of overheated rock, but went on to surprise researchers who feared its imminent demise, clinging on to the mountain for two more decades. In the last five years, which includes Europe’s three hottest years on record, the remaining ice has melted to a handful of isolated pockets, with the final remnant of the main body measuring just a few metres by the end of summer. pages.text: Small Business Owners | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Small Business Owners Thinking about offering a retirement plan for your workers? We're here to help. On this webpage, you’ll find links to publications and resources to learn more. You can also get help online or by calling 1-866-444-3272 . Your workforce is your most valuable resource. Attracting and keeping good employees by offering them a retirement plan is good for your business. It’s also good for your bottom line, since many retirement plans offer tax advantages to both employers and employees. Offering a retirement plan doesn’t have to be complicated. By setting up a system that fits your business’ needs, paying attention to make sure your plan is working properly, and having reasonable investments, you can help your employees —and yourself— save for retirement. So where do you start? Choosing a Plan That Fits Your Needs Browse plan options offering different levels of employer involvement, costs, and responsibilities. Understanding Your Responsibilities Learn what you need to do to get the plan up and running. Working With Service Providers Find out how to choose and monitor service providers and plan operations. pages.text: Small Business Pulse Survey: Tracking Changes During The Coronavirus Pandemic Small Business Pulse Survey: Tracking Changes During The Coronavirus Pandemic Skip Navigation Small Business Pulse Survey: Tracking Changes During The Coronavirus Pandemic February 11, 2022 The Small Business Pulse Survey (SBPS) measures the effect of changing business conditions during the Coronavirus pandemic on our nation's small businesses. SBPS data complements existing U.S. Census Bureau data collections by providing high-frequency, detailed information on the challenges small businesses are facing during the Coronavirus pandemic. Data is available by sector and state for the fifty most populous Metropolitan Statistical Areas (MSAs). Survey results give local, state, and federal officials essential real-time data to aid in policy and decision-making. In addition, the information aids businesses in making economic decisions and assists researchers studying the effects of the pandemic. SBPS results are experimental data products and are subject to suppression based on overall response and disclosure avoidance thresholds. Data products may not meet some of the Census Bureau’s statistical quality standards. Data tabulations and visualizations from ​the current and previous collection periods are available by clicking the “View Published Results” button. But small businesses employ disabled people at a much lower rate than do large companies. The Employer Assistance and Resource Network on Disability's (EARN) Small Business Toolkit was developed to help address this issue. The web-based toolkit provides small businesses with practical guidance on recruiting and retaining qualified people with disabilities. It further describes the advantages of recruiting, hiring, retaining and advancing disabled workers in small business. Extensive resources also provide cost effective and practical strategies.
